opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because my own path went through both worlds. I started in physics-based simulation and character animation, where you think carefully about dynamics, contact, and optimization. Then I moved into learning-based control, especially reinforcement learning for legged locomotion and sim-to-real transfer. So I've seen firsthand what each approach is good at and where it breaks down.

Traditional control is beautiful when you understand the system well. If you have a good model of the robot's dynamics, model predictive control or whole-body control gives you stability, interpretability, and guarantees. But when contact gets complicated, or the environment becomes unstructured, like grass, gravel, or stairs you've never seen, hand-designed models and hand-crafted state machines struggle. That's where reinforcement learning really surprised us. A policy trained in simulation, with enough domain randomization, could discover behaviors that would have taken engineers months to design, and it was often more robust.

What I learned, though, is that early on, combining the two was often the practical answer. You let learning handle the parts that are hard to model and keep structure where structure helps. That's essentially a hierarchical view: a high-level module decides what to do, and a lower-level controller, learned or classical, decides how to do it.

But my view has shifted over time. Hierarchies have a fundamental problem: the interfaces between layers are designed by humans. Whatever you choose to pass between the planner and the controller, a target velocity, a footstep location, an end-effector pose, becomes a bottleneck. Information that doesn't fit through that interface is lost, and errors in each layer compound. In the language model world, we've seen again and again that when you have enough data and compute, end-to-end systems win over carefully engineered pipelines. I think robotics is starting to go through the same transition. With vision-language-action models, you can have one model that goes from pixels and language to actions, and it can pick up the subtle correlations a hand-designed interface would throw away.

That said, I don't think it's black and white today. The biggest constraint in robotics is data. We don't have an internet of robot actions. So in practice, there's still a role for structure. For example, a large model reasoning at a slower frequency and a fast, reactive low-level policy running at hundreds of hertz, because physics demands that speed and big models can't yet run that fast on board. You could call that hierarchical, but increasingly both parts are learned and trained jointly, so the boundary becomes soft rather than hand-designed.

So my summary is: control theory taught me to respect physics and structure, and reinforcement learning taught me not to underestimate what learning can discover. Long term, I believe in unified, end-to-end models, because that's what scales. In the short term, the smartest approach is to use structure as scaffolding where data is scarce, and gradually remove it as data and compute catch up.

r001.rationale: The response says combining learning and structure was practical, but does not say this produced immediate gains because the traditional controller already largely worked.

r002.rationale: The response says hierarchical interfaces create bottlenecks and that unified, end-to-end models are what scale in the long term, while structure serves as short-term scaffolding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my background is actually in classical control and physics-based animation, and I came to reinforcement learning relatively late, which I think gives me a slightly different lens than people who started in deep learning.

When I was doing traditional control, everything was hierarchical by necessity. You had a planner that reasoned about where the robot should go, a trajectory optimizer that turned that into a feasible motion, and then a low-level controller, maybe a PD controller or some model-based whole-body controller, that tracked it at a thousand hertz. Each layer had a clear interface, clear assumptions, and you could analyze each piece. That was the strength. The weakness was that the interfaces were designed by humans, and every time the real world violated one of those assumptions, the whole stack became brittle. A legged robot would step on something unexpected and the trajectory optimizer's contact schedule would just be wrong.

What reinforcement learning showed me, especially in our early work on legged locomotion with sim-to-real, was that if you let the policy learn directly from proprioception to motor commands, it would discover behaviors that I would never have hand-designed. It would learn to recover from slips in ways that cut across all those layers I used to separate. That was genuinely surprising to me, and it made me much more sympathetic to the end-to-end view.

But I don't think it's a binary choice, and my view now is more nuanced than it was five years ago. The question I ask is: where does the structure come from? In a hierarchical system, humans impose the structure. In an end-to-end system, the structure has to emerge from data, and that's extremely expensive if the task is long-horizon. If you want a robot to walk across a room, open a fridge, and bring you a drink, the low-level balance problem and the high-level task reasoning problem live at completely different timescales and completely different levels of abstraction. Forcing a single network to learn both from scratch with the same gradient signal is wasteful.

So what we've converged on, and what I think a lot of the field is converging on, is something like a learned hierarchy. The low-level controller is still learned, often with RL in simulation, and it's extremely robust. The high-level layer is increasingly a foundation model, a language model or a vision-language model, that operates at a much lower frequency and reasons about tasks semantically. The key difference from the classical hierarchy is that the interface between them is also learned or at least is very flexible. Instead of a hand-designed trajectory, the high level might emit a latent skill, or a language instruction, or a target that the low level knows how to track robustly.

The other thing control theory left me with is a healthy respect for the low-level loop. Those fast feedback loops are where safety lives. Even in a unified model, I want some component that responds in milliseconds and does not depend on a large model finishing its inference. Whether you call that hierarchical or just good engineering, I think it's going to stay with us for a long time.

So my honest answer is that end-to-end is a very productive research direction because it tells us what structure is actually necessary versus what we imposed out of habit. But the systems that actually work on real robots today, and probably for a while, are hierarchical in spirit with the layers being learned rather than hand-written.

r001.rationale: The response describes learned policies discovering robust behaviors and improving recovery, but does not say that combining RL with traditional control produced immediate gains because the traditional controller already largely worked.

r002.rationale: The response calls end-to-end a productive research direction, but says systems that work today are hierarchical in spirit. It does not suggest unified models may ultimately outperform hierarchical shortcuts.

astra-6.text:
I see hierarchical and end-to-end approaches as two useful ways of deciding what structure we give a robot and what we ask it to learn. Traditional control gives us a lot of useful structure: ways to reason about stability, constraints, and how the system responds. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to handle behavior that is difficult to capture in a model or design by hand.

Combining them makes me pragmatic about hierarchy. You might let a learned policy decide what motion to execute, while a lower-level controller handles tracking. That separation makes it easier to diagnose failures and use what we already know about the physics. But the interface can also become a limitation. If the high-level policy can only issue a narrow set of commands, it may never discover a better way to move.

The attraction of end-to-end learning is that you can optimize the whole behavior together. The challenge is making that behavior reliable, understanding where it fails, and getting enough relevant training experience.

So I would choose based on the task and the evidence. Where structure improves reliability or makes learning more efficient, use it. Where a hand-designed boundary limits performance, consider learning across that boundary. To me, the interesting question is how much structure helps—and when it starts getting in the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes useful structure from traditional control, but does not say combining it with reinforcement learning produced immediate gains because the existing controller already largely worked.

r002.rationale: The response notes that hierarchy can limit performance and that learning across boundaries may help, but does not suggest end-to-end or unified models will ultimately outperform hierarchical shortcuts for near-term results.

sol-6.1.text:
My experience has made me fairly pragmatic about this. Traditional control gives us useful structure: we know how to reason about stability, dynamics, and constraints. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to handle things that are difficult to model explicitly, such as complex contact or adapting a behavior through experience. Combining them can make a robot much easier to train and debug.

That’s a strong argument for hierarchy. A learned policy might decide where to move or what motion to execute, while a controller handles tracking and some of the physical constraints. But the interfaces matter. If we choose an interface that’s too restrictive, the learning algorithm can’t discover a better solution, even if it has enough data.

End-to-end learning is attractive because it can optimize across those boundaries. The challenge is making that optimization reliable, data-efficient, and transferable to a real robot. So I don’t think there’s one architecture that wins everywhere. I would use the structure we understand well, while allowing learning to take on more responsibility as the evidence supports it. And an end-to-end trained system can still have hierarchy inside it; those ideas aren’t necessarily in conflict.

r001.rationale: It says combining control and reinforcement learning can make robots easier to train and debug, but does not say this produced immediate gains because the traditional controller already largely worked.

r002.rationale: It notes end-to-end learning can optimize across boundaries, but does not suggest it will ultimately outperform hierarchical approaches; it says no architecture wins everywhere.
